title: Heat Stroke: Altered Mental Status Makes It an Emergency
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: Heat stroke is life-threatening hyperthermia with CNS dysfunction. Start emergency cooling and activate emergency response rather than treating it like routine dehydration.
recognize: Confusion, collapse, seizures, ataxia, very high body temperature, hot skin, tachycardia, and hypotension can occur.
priorities: Activate emergency care, remove from heat, begin rapid cooling, and protect airway/ABC status.
assessMonitor: Trend temperature, mental status, vitals, glucose, urine output, and signs of rhabdomyolysis/organ injury.
interventions: Use rapid external cooling per emergency protocol and avoid delaying cooling for nonessential testing.
medicationSafety: Antipyretics do not correct heat stroke because the mechanism is not a hypothalamic fever set-point problem.
teaching: Heat illness risk rises with exertion, dehydration, older age, and certain medications; prevention plans matter during extreme heat.
delegationScope: Emergency cooling/support may be initiated per protocol; unstable patients require immediate RN/provider/EMS escalation.
examTrap: Giving acetaminophen and waiting for the temperature to fall.
oneLinePearl: Hot plus confused equals emergency cooling.

title: Hypothermia: Handle Gently and Rewarm Safely
bottomLine: Moderate or severe hypothermia can cause bradycardia, dysrhythmias, altered mental status, and impaired coagulation. Remove wet clothing, insulate, rewarm according to severity, and handle unstable patients gently.
recognize: Shivering may disappear as hypothermia worsens; confusion, slurred speech, poor coordination, bradycardia, and reduced consciousness are danger signs.
priorities: Prevent further heat loss, assess ABCs, and escalate significant hypothermia or instability.
assessMonitor: Core temperature when available, rhythm, mental status, glucose, perfusion, and frostbite/trauma.
interventions: Use passive/active rewarming per protocol and avoid unnecessary rough movement in severe hypothermia.
medicationSafety: Drug metabolism may be altered in severe hypothermia; advanced resuscitation medication decisions follow emergency protocols.
redFlags: No shivering with severe cold exposure
teaching: Layer clothing, stay dry, and seek help early when confusion or severe shivering occurs.
delegationScope: Basic warming measures may be implemented within protocol; unstable hypothermia requires emergency escalation.
examTrap: Massaging cold extremities aggressively to warm the patient faster.
oneLinePearl: Cold hearts are irritable—rewarm and handle gently.

title: Carbon Monoxide: Normal Pulse Oximetry Can Mislead
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: Carbon monoxide poisoning causes headache, dizziness, nausea, weakness, chest symptoms, and neurologic change and may affect several people in the same location. Standard pulse oximetry can appear reassuring despite serious exposure.
recognize: Multiple household members with similar flu-like symptoms without fever, generator/heater exposure, syncope, confusion, or chest pain are important clues.
priorities: Remove from exposure, provide high-concentration oxygen per emergency guidance, and escalate for confirmatory testing/medical evaluation.
assessMonitor: Neurologic status, cardiac symptoms, exposure history, pregnancy status when relevant, carboxyhemoglobin testing, and ECG/labs as ordered.
interventions: Continue oxygen and serial neurologic assessment per emergency plan.
medicationSafety: Do not use a normal pulse-oximeter reading to withhold oxygen when CO poisoning is suspected.
teaching: Never use generators, grills, or fuel-burning devices indoors or near openings into occupied spaces.
delegationScope: Emergency oxygen/support follows protocol; diagnostic and hyperbaric decisions are provider-level.
examTrap: Ruling out CO poisoning because SpO2 reads 99%.
oneLinePearl: CO can fool the pulse oximeter—trust the exposure story and symptoms.
sourceBasis: CDC Carbon Monoxide Poisoning clinical guidance

title: Drowning: Hypoxia Comes Before the Water Story
bottomLine: The immediate danger after drowning is hypoxia. Prioritize rescue breathing/CPR as indicated, oxygenation, and rapid evaluation rather than attempts to remove water from the lungs.
recognize: Cough, respiratory distress, hypoxemia, altered mental status, apnea, or cardiac arrest can follow submersion.
priorities: Ensure scene safety, activate EMS, assess breathing/pulse, and begin resuscitation per current guidelines.
assessMonitor: Respiratory effort, oxygenation, mental status, temperature, trauma, and delayed pulmonary deterioration.
interventions: Provide oxygen/ventilatory support and rewarming as indicated.
medicationSafety: Do not give prophylactic antibiotics routinely without a specific clinical indication/provider decision.
teaching: Any significant respiratory or neurologic symptoms after submersion require urgent evaluation.
delegationScope: Basic life support follows certification; advanced interventions require appropriate credentialing.
examTrap: Using abdominal thrusts to expel water before starting ventilation/CPR.
oneLinePearl: After drowning, oxygenation is the rescue priority.

title: Lightning Injury: Cardiac and Neurologic Effects Can Be Immediate
bottomLine: Lightning can cause cardiac arrest, respiratory arrest, neurologic injury, burns, tympanic injury, and trauma. Victims do not retain an electrical charge and are safe to touch for rescue.
recognize: Unresponsiveness, arrhythmia, paralysis, confusion, burns, hearing injury, or blunt trauma may follow a strike.
priorities: Ensure scene safety, begin CPR/AED when needed, and prioritize apparently pulseless/apneic victims because successful resuscitation is possible.
assessMonitor: Cardiac rhythm, neurologic status, respiratory function, burns, hearing, vision, and trauma.
interventions: Provide BLS/advanced care and trauma evaluation as indicated.
medicationSafety: No medication substitutes for immediate resuscitation and rhythm management.
teaching: Seek substantial shelter during thunderstorms; avoid isolated trees and open areas.
delegationScope: BLS follows certification; advanced cardiac/trauma care requires appropriate personnel.
examTrap: Avoiding contact with the victim because you think they are still electrically charged.
oneLinePearl: Lightning victims are safe to touch—resuscitate immediately.

title: Chemical Exposure: Protect Yourself Before Decontaminating the Patient
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: Chemical contamination can harm rescuers and spread into the care environment. Use appropriate PPE, remove the patient from exposure when safe, and follow substance-specific decontamination guidance.
recognize: Odor, visible residue, multiple affected people, burning eyes/skin, coughing, vomiting, or neurologic symptoms may indicate hazardous exposure.
priorities: Protect staff/bystanders, activate hazardous-material resources, and prevent secondary contamination.
assessMonitor: Airway/breathing, skin/eye injury, neurologic status, exposure substance/route/duration, and contamination status.
interventions: Remove contaminated clothing and irrigate/decontaminate according to poison-control/hazmat guidance when appropriate.
medicationSafety: Do not give an antidote unless the specific exposure and protocol/order support it.
teaching: Call poison control/emergency services for significant exposures rather than using unverified home neutralization methods.
delegationScope: Hazmat/decontamination roles depend on facility training and PPE capability.
examTrap: Running into a contaminated area without PPE to help faster.
oneLinePearl: Do not become the second patient.

title: Mass-Casualty Triage: Greatest Good for the Greatest Number
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Coordinated Care
Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: Disaster triage differs from routine bedside prioritization. Use the incident-command/triage system to rapidly identify who needs immediate lifesaving intervention, who can wait, and who can safely self-ambulate to lower-acuity care.
recognize: Resource scarcity and multiple casualties change the goal from maximizing one patient's care to maximizing overall survival.
priorities: Follow the designated disaster-triage algorithm and incident command rather than creating an individual system.
assessMonitor: Airway/breathing/perfusion/mental status and immediate lifesaving intervention needs according to the selected system.
interventions: Tag/communicate category, perform only permitted rapid lifesaving interventions, and move patients according to command.
medicationSafety: Do not consume scarce medications/supplies on low-benefit interventions that conflict with the disaster plan.
teaching: Community disaster plans should include medications, contacts, evacuation routes, and communication plans.
delegationScope: Triage role depends on incident command, licensure, and disaster credentialing; follow assigned scope.
examTrap: Applying ordinary first-come-first-served care during a mass-casualty event.
oneLinePearl: Disaster triage prioritizes survivability and scarce resources.

title: Generator Safety: Prevent Carbon Monoxide During Outages
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Safety and Infection Control
bottomLine: Portable generators and fuel-burning devices can cause lethal carbon monoxide accumulation during outages. Never operate them inside homes, garages, basements, campers, or near openings into occupied spaces.
recognize: Power outage plus headache, nausea, dizziness, confusion, or several ill household members should trigger CO concern.
priorities: Move to fresh air, call emergency services when symptoms/exposure are significant, and do not re-enter unsafe spaces.
assessMonitor: Exposure source, symptoms, other household members, and CO-alarm status.
interventions: Use functioning CO alarms and manufacturer/emergency guidance for safe generator placement.
medicationSafety: People dependent on electrically powered medication devices/oxygen equipment need outage plans before emergencies.
redFlags: Generator operating in/near enclosed occupied space
teaching: Generators belong outdoors and away from windows/doors/vents; test CO alarms regularly.
delegationScope: Community teaching can be reinforced by PN/LVN staff within role.
examTrap: Running a generator in an attached garage with the door open.
oneLinePearl: An open garage is still not a safe generator location.
sourceBasis: CDC Carbon Monoxide generator-safety guidance updated 2026

title: Smoke Exposure: Respiratory Injury Can Worsen After the Fire
bottomLine: Enclosed-space smoke exposure can produce airway edema, carbon monoxide toxicity, bronchospasm, and systemic toxic exposures even when external burns are minor. Respiratory deterioration can evolve over time.
recognize: Hoarseness, soot, facial burns, cough, wheeze, stridor, confusion, headache, and enclosed-space exposure are concerning.
priorities: Escalate airway/oxygenation risk early and administer emergency oxygen/support per protocol.
assessMonitor: Voice/airway, respiratory effort, SpO2 in context, mental status, CO exposure, burns, and evolving edema.
interventions: Prepare for advanced airway evaluation when swelling/respiratory distress progresses.
medicationSafety: Normal pulse oximetry does not exclude carbon monoxide poisoning.
teaching: Seek emergency evaluation after significant enclosed-space smoke exposure when respiratory or neurologic symptoms occur.
delegationScope: Unstable airway assessment/escalation requires licensed/emergency clinicians.
examTrap: Being reassured by small skin burns while ignoring hoarseness and soot.
oneLinePearl: The airway can be the biggest burn you cannot see.

title: Disaster Medication Continuity: Plan Before the Supply Chain Breaks
clientNeeds: Safe and Effective Care Environment: Coordinated Care
bottomLine: Disasters can interrupt access to insulin, oxygen, dialysis, anticoagulants, antiseizure drugs, psychiatric medications, and refrigeration/electricity-dependent therapies. Emergency planning should identify which medications/devices cannot safely be interrupted.
recognize: Limited refill supply, refrigeration dependence, powered devices, controlled substances, dialysis, and specialty pharmacy access increase vulnerability.
priorities: Maintain an updated medication list, emergency contacts, backup power/storage plan, and clinician/pharmacy instructions.
assessMonitor: Days of supply, storage requirements, device battery/power needs, evacuation destination, and high-risk interruption consequences.
interventions: Coordinate early with pharmacy/provider/emergency services when access is threatened; use approved emergency-refill pathways.
medicationSafety: Do not ration or substitute critical medications independently unless directed by an emergency treatment plan.
redFlags: No safe refrigeration for required therapy
teaching: Keep a written medication/device list and disaster kit and know where to obtain emergency care/refills.
delegationScope: PN/LVN staff may reinforce preparedness teaching and escalate medication-access risks to the care team.
examTrap: Waiting until the last dose is gone before contacting the pharmacy or emergency plan.
oneLinePearl: Disaster medication safety starts before the disaster.
